assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, turned optical frequency standards into many-atom, low-uncertainty devices at the 10^-18 level. It is an original idea with a concrete payoff: the most precise measurements made by humans, opening tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice concept; Jun Ye's group brought the strontium clock to record accuracy and developed its systematics control. The two-name credit is clean. Other clock groups (ion clocks, other lattice groups) are not in the supplied credit and are outside the entry as framed.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: multiple independent laboratories confirm 10^-18 performance and clock comparisons across institutes are routine. Recognition is timely given the planned redefinition of the second, and the 2005 prize for the frequency comb leaves this step unrecognized.
uncertainties: The relative credit between Katori and Ye, and the roles of other lattice-clock groups, is a judgement I cannot verify from the supplied text.
Whether the committee would prefer to recognise ion clocks or the redefinition of the second jointly is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum computing with trapped ions, and the subsequent theory of quantum simulation with trapped ions and ultracold atoms, supplied the blueprint for controllable quantum many-body devices. The ideas are original, clearly stated and have shaped experiments on ions, neutral atoms and Rydberg arrays for three decades.
assessment.attribution: A clean two-person theory prize with decisive and well-documented contributions by both. The experimental realisation by ion groups (Wineland, Blatt and others) is partly recognised already by the 2012 prize, which makes a theory-focused citation a natural complement. Overlap with candidates on optical-lattice simulation (B056) and Rydberg arrays (B004) would have to be resolved in citation wording.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: the proposals were tested repeatedly and implemented in several platforms, and the field has gone from proposals to commercial hardware. Recognition is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a narrower trapped-ion gate citation or a broader quantum-simulation citation that adds more people.
I cannot verify exactly how much later gate schemes (such as Molmer-Sorensen) displace the original Cirac-Zoller gate in practice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire flat-band physics, with correlated insulators and superconductivity at tunable density in a simple carbon system. The prediction of flat bands at a magic angle followed by experimental discovery is a classic theory-to-experiment story, and the impact on condensed matter has been very large and rapid.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model (2011) predicted the flat bands; the Jarillo-Herrero group reported the correlated and superconducting states in 2018. A three-person prize fits that story. Contributions from Cory Dean's group on hBN-based devices and from other twistronics theorists are not in the supplied credit; related candidate B017 (hBN crystals) overlaps.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups and many device geometries within a few years, but the microscopic origin of superconductivity is still debated, and the field is still moving. Recognition might be slightly early but the discovery itself is secure.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states are unresolved, so the citation would have to focus on the flat-band prediction and the observation.
The place of early experimental precursors and of other theorists is not settled by the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The LHC and its general-purpose detectors enabled the discovery of the Higgs boson and a decade of precision exploration of the Standard Model at the TeV scale. It is an extraordinary experimental achievement of enormous scale, and the 2013 prize recognised the theory of the mechanism but not the experiments.
assessment.attribution: Evans led machine construction; Della Negra and Jenni are founding figures of CMS and ATLAS. The three-person credit is workable but necessarily omits many leaders, such as spokespersons and the physicists who made the discovery. The Nobel statutes favour a discovery or invention, and the choice between honouring the machine and detectors or the discovery itself (B055) is a real allocation problem.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: the Higgs discovery has been confirmed with precise coupling measurements by both experiments, and the machine continues to run. Timing is acceptable, although the prize for the discovery itself is long awaited.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to honour the discovery (B055) rather than the instruments.
The fairness of a three-name credit for collaborations of thousands is a persistent difficulty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a new class of quantum matter, with protected edge and surface states. The theoretical idea is original and the experimental confirmation in HgTe is clear. It has stimulated a large body of work on topological materials.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele predicted the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene (2005) and the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group observed it in HgTe quantum wells (2007) following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The supplied credit omits the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and the Fu-Kane three-dimensional work, so a fair configuration is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independently confirmed in several materials, and extended to three dimensions and to topological crystalline phases. The 2016 prize for topological phase transitions covers a related but different step, and recognition now would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the supplied credit can support a fair prize without the BHZ prediction and the Fu-Kane work.
Technological relevance of the quantum spin Hall edge states has so far been limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube detected a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and then evidence of a blazar source and the galactic plane. This opened a new window on the high-energy universe, achieved by an ambitious cubic-kilometre detector built in Antarctic ice.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube and the earlier AMANDA experiment; Spiering was a long-time leader of the collaboration's physics programme. As with other large experiments, a two-name credit is unavoidably partial. John Learned and others who initiated neutrino astronomy are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature: the diffuse flux has been confirmed by other analyses and by other experiments, and source identification is advancing, but individual sources remain few and the origin of the bulk of the flux is unexplained. A prize could be seen as slightly early.
uncertainties: The sources of most of the observed neutrinos are not identified.
The fairness of a two-name credit for a very large collaboration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision (three-step) model is the conceptual foundation for high-harmonic generation and attosecond science: ionisation, acceleration in the laser field and recombination, with its quantum counterpart. It is simple, original and quantitatively predictive. Because the 2023 prize recognised experimental generation of attosecond pulses, a further prize for the theory would have to be justified as distinct recognition.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's 1993 model is the central contribution; Schafer, Kulander and co-workers published a closely contemporaneous numerical and semiclassical account, and the Lewenstein et al. 1994 strong-field approximation provided the quantum theory. Kenneth Kulander is not in the supplied credit, and the credit among the three-step ideas is a known question. I note, as a disclosure, that I work in this area and have collaborated with members of the attosecond community (for example Anne L'Huillier), which I would treat as a conflict.
assessment.maturity: Mature and universally used, tested in a great many experiments. But recognition is arguably partly delivered by the 2023 prize, so the case for timeliness is weaker than for a wholly unrecognised discovery.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 prize may make a second prize in this area unattractive.
Credit allocation between Corkum, the Kulander-Schafer group and Lewenstein, and the absence of Kulander from the supplied names.
My own proximity to the area limits how independently I can judge it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84) founded quantum cryptography, using quantum mechanics itself to secure communication. The idea is original and clear and has led to a field with commercial and satellite demonstrations. It is a natural counterpart to the 2022 prize on entanglement and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the originators of BB84. Ekert's entanglement-based protocol (1991) is a separate and important contribution and appears twice in the credited list under two spellings (Artur Ekert and Artur K. Ekert), which I treat as one person. I propose only Bennett and Brassard, which leaves the question of Ekert unresolved. I would not add a third name from the duplicate entry without clarifying it.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a concept and experimentally demonstrated over long distances, but practical security against implementation attacks is an ongoing engineering matter, and large-scale deployment is limited. The idea has been understood for decades, so the recognition is timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether Ekert should share credit alongside Bennett and Brassard.
Whether the committee regards quantum cryptography as physics or as information science or engineering.
